title: Attack rate, relative risk, and confounding

blocks.text: Everyone who ate the potato salad got sick. But so did a lot of people who didn't. How do you decide which food is the real culprit?

chunks.text: The **attack rate** is the proportion of people at risk who became ill: cases ÷ people exposed. Compare the attack rate in people who had an exposure to the attack rate in people who did not.

**Relative risk** (RR) = attack rate in the exposed ÷ attack rate in the unexposed. An RR far above 1 points to a likely culprit. But beware **confounding**: a third factor linked to both the exposure and the illness can create a fake link.

steps.caption: Count who ate the food and who got sick in a 2×2 table.
nodes: Did not eat it: 4 ill, 36 not ill

steps.caption: Attack rate in those who ate it: 40 ÷ 60 = 67%. In those who did not: 4 ÷ 40 = 10%.
Relative risk = 67% ÷ 10% ≈ 6.7. The food is a strong suspect, but check for confounders.

blocks.title: Worked example: a confounder
steps: Situation: festival-goers have an RR of 2 for illness.
But nearly all the sick people live in Old Town, and Old Town residents are more likely to attend.
Compare festival-goers and non-goers inside Old Town.
If the RR within Old Town is near 1, then neighborhood (not the festival) explains the link: confounding.

bullets: Relative risk = exposed attack rate ÷ unexposed attack rate.
A high RR suggests a link; it does not prove cause.
A confounder is tied to both exposure and illness; compare within groups to check.
